name: The Hershey-Chase Experiment
statement: By tagging a virus's DNA and protein separately, Hershey and Chase showed it is the DNA that carries heredity.
statementAccent: showed it is the DNA that carries heredity
meaning: The Hershey-Chase experiment was a set of experiments performed by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase in 1952 at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, which provided strong confirmation that DNA, rather than protein, is the genetic material that carries hereditary information. They worked with a bacteriophage, a virus that infects bacteria, specifically the T2 phage that infects the bacterium Escherichia coli. A phage consists essentially of a protein coat surrounding a core of DNA, and the question was which of these two components enters the bacterium to direct the production of new viruses. To find out, Hershey and Chase labelled the two components with different radioactive tracers: they tagged the DNA with radioactive phosphorus, which is present in DNA but not in protein, and the protein with radioactive sulfur, which is present in protein but not in DNA. After letting the labelled phages infect bacteria, they used a kitchen blender to shear the empty phage coats off the outside of the bacteria and spun the mixture in a centrifuge to separate the cells from the coats. They found that the radioactive phosphorus, marking the DNA, had entered the bacteria, while most of the radioactive sulfur, marking the protein, remained outside. This showed that DNA is the material that enters the cell and carries the genetic instructions.
mechanism: The experiment distinguished DNA from protein by tagging each with a radioactive element unique to it and tracking where each went during infection. Because DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, and protein contains sulfur but essentially no phosphorus, Hershey and Chase grew two batches of T2 phage, one in a medium with radioactive phosphorus-32 to label the DNA and one with radioactive sulfur-35 to label the protein coat. Each batch of labelled phage was then allowed to infect fresh, unlabelled E. coli bacteria, attaching to the cell surface and injecting whatever component carries the genetic information. After allowing time for infection, they agitated the mixture in a Waring blender, which sheared the spent phage coats off the outside of the bacteria without breaking the cells open, and then centrifuged the suspension so that the heavier bacterial cells collected in a pellet at the bottom while the lighter phage coats stayed in the liquid above. Measuring the radioactivity in each fraction, they found the phosphorus-32, and thus the DNA, chiefly inside the bacterial pellet and passed on to the next generation of phages, while most of the sulfur-35, and thus the protein, remained in the coats outside. DNA, therefore, was the material that entered the cell to direct the making of new virus.

examples.text: Phosphorus-32 labelled the DNA, which contains phosphorus but no sulfur, and sulfur-35 labelled the protein, which contains sulfur but no phosphorus.
A Waring blender sheared the empty phage coats off the bacteria, and centrifuging separated the cells from the coats.
The radioactive phosphorus, marking the DNA, was found inside the bacteria, while the sulfur-marked protein stayed outside.

variants.name: Phage as the tool
variants.text: The use of the T2 bacteriophage, a simple virus of protein and DNA, to ask which component carries heredity into the cell.

variants.name: Confirmation of Avery
variants.text: The experiment as strong confirmation of the earlier Avery-MacLeod-McCarty finding that DNA is the genetic material.

whyItMatters: The Hershey-Chase experiment is a landmark in the history of biology because it provided decisive, widely accepted evidence that DNA is the molecule of heredity, resolving a long-standing question about whether genes are made of protein or of DNA. Although the Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment had already pointed to DNA in 1944, many scientists remained skeptical, favouring protein because DNA seemed too simple to carry the complexity of life; the clear, elegant Hershey-Chase result, showing that it is the phage's DNA and not its protein that enters the cell to produce new virus, helped convince the field. Coming just a year before Watson and Crick revealed the double-helix structure of DNA, it helped set the stage for the molecular revolution in biology, in which DNA became the central molecule of genetics. The experiment is also celebrated for its clever design, using radioactive tracers and a common kitchen blender to answer a fundamental question. Hershey shared the 1969 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the genetics of viruses.

working.text: grow phage with radioactive phosphorus to tag DNA and radioactive sulfur to tag the protein coat.
let the labelled phage infect bacteria, then shear the coats off with a blender and separate cells from coats by centrifuging.
find the phosphorus, and thus the DNA, inside the cells and the sulfur-tagged protein outside, showing DNA carries heredity.

limits: The Hershey-Chase experiment was persuasive but not perfectly clean, so its result is best described as strong confirmation rather than airtight proof on its own. The separation was imperfect: some radioactive sulfur, and thus protein, was carried into the cells, and some phosphorus-tagged DNA remained outside, so the distinction between inside and outside was a matter of proportion, not an absolute divide. The experiment was as influential as it was partly because the field was already moving toward accepting DNA, building on the earlier Avery-MacLeod-McCarty work, which it complemented and reinforced. It concerned a simple bacteriophage, and generalizing to all life rested on further evidence. Hershey's 1969 Nobel Prize was shared with Delbrück and Luria and cited their broader work on the genetics of viruses rather than this experiment alone.
misreadings: The Hershey-Chase experiment did not single-handedly or perfectly prove DNA is the genetic material; the separation was imperfect, with some protein entering the cells, so it strengthened rather than clinched the case. It was not the first evidence, since the Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment had pointed to DNA in 1944, which it confirmed. And it studied a simple virus, so extending the conclusion to all life needed further work, so treating the experiment as flawless, as the sole proof, or as immediately universal, misreads a pivotal confirmation that DNA carries heredity.
origin: Experiments by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase in 1952 at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, using radioactively labelled bacteriophage to show that DNA, not protein, enters the bacterium and carries heredity; strong confirmation that DNA is the genetic material.
